analysis.one_liner: Raises required overtime pay from time-and-a-half to double time.
analysis.headline: A bill to double overtime pay for millions of hourly workers was introduced in June 2026 with 30 cosponsors, all Democrats, and was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where it has not moved.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill amends the Fair Labor Standards Act so that employers must pay two times a worker's regular rate for overtime hours, instead of the current one and one-half times [S2]. It covers overtime across the law, including the special overtime rules for hospitals, seamen, and other covered industries, and takes effect 180 days after enactment [S2]. A worker putting in 10 overtime hours at a $20 wage would earn $400 for those hours instead of $300. The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and has had no further action [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly workers who put in overtime hours would see that extra time paid at double their regular rate instead of time-and-a-half, a 33% raise on every overtime hour [S2]. Workers in industries with long or unpredictable hours — manufacturing, logistics, retail, food service, construction — would gain the most.

how_it_helps.text: Rewrites the Fair Labor Standards Act to replace 'one and one-half' with 'two' everywhere the overtime rate appears, so covered overtime hours must be paid at twice the regular rate [S2].
Applies the doubled rate to the special overtime provisions for hospitals, seamen, and other covered employment as well as the general overtime rule, and takes effect 180 days after enactment [S2].
Was introduced with 18 original cosponsors and reached 30 total cosponsors, all House Democrats [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers of hourly workers would bear higher payroll costs on every overtime hour, which would fall most heavily on labor-intensive businesses that rely on extended shifts — manufacturers, warehouses, retailers, restaurants, hospitals, and contractors. Small businesses with thin margins would face the same increase as large firms, with less room to absorb it.

drawbacks.text: The higher rate directly raises labor costs on overtime hours; employers facing a 2x rate may respond by scheduling fewer overtime hours, meaning some workers could see their overtime opportunities shrink even as each remaining overtime hour pays more [S2].

The doubling applies across nearly all covered employment with no phase-in beyond 180 days or carve-outs for small businesses, so employers with the thinnest margins face the full increase quickly [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers who currently log overtime hours, the benefit is straightforward: every overtime hour pays about a third more. The real trade-off is on the employer side — a doubled rate gives businesses a much stronger incentive to cap hours at 40, so some workers may lose access to overtime pay entirely. Whether workers come out ahead depends on how many keep their overtime hours versus how much the remaining hours pay. The bill offers no small-business accommodation or gradual phase-in beyond the 180-day delay, which makes the adjustment sharper for low-margin employers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which has not taken it up; no hearing, markup, or floor vote is scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Greg Casar introduced the bill on June 9, 2026, with 18 original cosponsors [S2].
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and Workforce the same day [S4].
The bill has accumulated 30 cosponsors, all House Democrats, with no Republican support listed [S3].
No further action has been recorded since the committee referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has won or lost — the bill sits in committee. If it never advances, employers of hourly workers are better off keeping overtime at time-and-a-half, and workers are no better off than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No outcome yet — pending in committee

for.name: Rep. Greg Casar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to double the overtime rate under the Fair Labor Standards Act.

for.name: 30 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsors signed on.

sides.party_line_note: All 30 cosponsors are House Democrats and no Republicans have signed on, though the bill has not yet received a vote that would show where the parties stand.

industries.industry: Retail, restaurant, and other employers of hourly workers
industries.note: Doubling the overtime rate raises their payroll cost on every overtime hour by about a third, which is exactly the money that would go to workers' paychecks. Their incentive to keep the current time-and-a-half rate runs directly against the workers' raise [S2].

The doubled rate applies to them on the same terms as large employers after a 180-day delay, with no small-business exemption, so the cost increase is proportionally harder for them to absorb. Workers' higher pay comes from these employers' schedules and margins [S2].

analysis.trajectory: Bills that reach only a committee referral and have no cosponsors from the majority party rarely get a hearing or a floor vote in the same Congress. With a Republican House majority of 223 members, no Republican cosponsors, and no committee action on record, the bill is very unlikely to advance further this session.
